title: How does Flink checkpointing work via barrier snapshots (barriers injected at sources flow through the graph, barrier alignment waits for a barrier on all inputs, then each task snapshots its state asynchronously to durable storage like S3/HDFS)?
shortTitle: How does Flink checkpointing work via barrier snapshots

s1_definition.profdef: Flink checkpointing is a distributed snapshot mechanism based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm. The JobManager's checkpoint coordinator periodically injects special records called checkpoint barriers into the stream at the sources. Each barrier carries a checkpoint id and flows downstream through the dataflow graph alongside normal records. When an operator with multiple inputs receives a barrier on one input, it performs barrier alignment, waiting until it has received the barrier for that checkpoint on all inputs, at which point it snapshots its own state asynchronously to durable storage such as S3 or HDFS and forwards the barrier downstream. When all operators have acknowledged, the checkpoint is complete and represents a globally consistent snapshot from which the job can recover with exactly-once semantics.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants a perfectly consistent photograph of its entire assembly line of clerks at one logical instant, without stopping the line. The checkpoint coordinator sends a special colored slip, the barrier, down each input conveyor. Each clerk keeps processing normal slips until the colored slip arrives. A clerk fed by two conveyors waits until the colored slip has arrived on both before taking a photo of their own passbook state, so the photo captures exactly the work done before the barrier and nothing after. Once a clerk has taken their photo, they pass the colored slip on to the next clerk. When every clerk has filed their photo, the bank has one coherent snapshot of the whole line taken as of that barrier, and if anything crashes it can restore every clerk to exactly that moment.
s1_definition.oneliner: Checkpoint barriers flow from sources through the graph, each operator aligns barriers across its inputs then snapshots its state asynchronously to durable storage, producing one globally consistent recovery point.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flink checkpointing is a distributed snapshot mechanism based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm. The JobManager's checkpoint coordinator periodically injects special records called checkpoint barriers into the stream at the sources. Each barrier carries a checkpoint id and flows downstream through the dataflow graph alongside normal records. When an operator with multiple inputs receives a barrier on one input, it performs barrier alignment, waiting until it has received the barrier for that checkpoint on all inputs, at which point it snapshots its own state asynchronously to durable storage such as S3 or HDFS and forwards the barrier downstream. When all operators have acknowledged, the checkpoint is complete and represents a globally consistent snapshot from which the job can recover with exactly-once semantics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants a perfectly consistent photograph of its entire assembly line of clerks at one logical instant, without stopping the line. The checkpoint coordinator sends a special colored slip, the barrier, down each input conveyor. Each clerk keeps processing normal slips until the colored slip arrives. A clerk fed by two conveyors waits until the colored slip has arrived on both before taking a photo of their own passbook state, so the photo captures exactly the work done before the barrier and nothing after. Once a clerk has taken their photo, they pass the colored slip on to the next clerk. When every clerk has filed their photo, the bank has one coherent snapshot of the whole line taken as of that barrier, and if anything crashes it can restore every clerk to exactly that moment.

**One line to remember:** Checkpoint barriers flow from sources through the graph, each operator aligns barriers across its inputs then snapshots its state asynchronously to durable storage, producing one globally consistent recovery point.

sections.s2_technical:
The checkpoint coordinator lives in the JobManager and triggers a checkpoint on a configured interval, for example `env.enableCheckpointing(10_000)` for every ten seconds. To start a checkpoint it tells every source to inject a barrier with the new checkpoint id into its output stream. A barrier is not data; it is a marker that separates the records that belong before the checkpoint from those that belong after it. Barriers flow downstream exactly like records, never overtaking them, so the ordering of records relative to the barrier is preserved on every channel.

When an operator has a single input, receiving the barrier simply means it snapshots its state and forwards the barrier. When an operator has multiple input channels, for example after a keyBy or a join, it must perform barrier alignment. As soon as the barrier arrives on one input channel, the operator stops consuming further records from that channel and buffers them, while it keeps consuming the other channels until their barriers for the same checkpoint also arrive. Once barriers have arrived on all input channels, the operator knows it has processed exactly all pre-checkpoint records and no post-checkpoint records, so it snapshots its state and then forwards a single barrier downstream and resumes consuming the buffered records. This alignment is what guarantees a consistent cut across the distributed graph.

The snapshot itself is written asynchronously. When an operator snapshots, it captures a copy of its state and hands it to a background process that uploads it to durable storage like S3 or HDFS, so the main processing thread is blocked only briefly, or not at all with copy-on-write state backends and asynchronous snapshots. Each operator acknowledges its completed snapshot to the coordinator. When the coordinator has received acknowledgments from every operator, it marks the checkpoint complete and records its metadata; only then is the checkpoint usable for recovery. On failure, Flink restarts the job, restores every operator's state from the last completed checkpoint, and rewinds the sources to the offsets recorded in that checkpoint, so processing resumes from a consistent point with exactly-once state semantics. The senior nuances are that barrier alignment can cause backpressure to amplify when one input is slow, because fast channels are buffered while waiting, which motivated unaligned checkpoints; that asynchronous snapshots keep the pipeline moving; and that exactly-once end-to-end additionally requires transactional or idempotent sinks, because checkpointing alone guarantees consistent state, not consistent external side effects.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a stateful job that maintains a running balance per account by consuming a transaction stream. If a task manager crashes, the bank cannot afford to either lose updates or double-apply them, because that would corrupt balances. It needs a globally consistent snapshot of all balances plus the exact source positions, taken without stopping the stream, so recovery resumes from one coherent instant. This is exactly what barrier-based checkpointing provides: a consistent cut across the whole job.

Problem 2 — One operator in the job merges two input streams, the retail transaction stream and the corporate transaction stream, and it must snapshot in a way that captures exactly the records before the barrier from both inputs and none after. If it snapshotted as soon as the first barrier arrived, it might include some post-barrier records from the faster stream and produce an inconsistent snapshot. This is exactly what barrier alignment solves: the operator waits for the barrier on both inputs before snapshotting.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that reproduces the barrier mechanics. We define a `Record` that is either a normal transaction or a `Barrier` carrying a checkpoint id. A `SourceOperator` injects barriers into its output on command. A `BalanceOperator` maintains per-account balances and, being single-input, snapshots and forwards when it sees a barrier. A `MergeOperator` has two inputs and performs barrier alignment, buffering the input that barriers first and waiting for the second before it snapshots. A `CheckpointCoordinator` triggers the barrier and collects acknowledgments, declaring the checkpoint complete only when all operators acknowledge, and can then restore the job. A `BarrierCheckpointDemo` main class streams transactions through both operators, triggers a checkpoint mid-stream, shows the merge operator aligning, shows the asynchronous snapshot and acknowledgments, then simulates a crash and restore from the completed checkpoint.

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  checkpoint:
    interval-ms: 10000
    mode: EXACTLY_ONCE          # alignment on
    timeout-ms: 60000
    storage: s3://nbi-flink/checkpoints
    min-pause-ms: 5000
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a few transactions flowing through a single-input balance operator and a two-input merge operator fed by a retail stream and a corporate stream, with a checkpoint triggered mid-stream.

Step 1: Before the checkpoint, the balance operator processes a 1000 credit for Rajesh and a 500 credit for Priya, updating its per-account state. The merge operator processes one retail transaction, incrementing its merged count. No barrier has been injected yet.

Step 2: The coordinator triggers checkpoint one and the source injects a barrier carrying checkpoint id one into the stream. The barrier is a marker, not data, and flows downstream behind the records that came before it.

Step 3: The barrier reaches the single-input balance operator. Because it has only one input, no alignment is needed: it immediately snapshots its current balances, acknowledges to the coordinator, and forwards the barrier. The snapshot captures Rajesh at 1000 and Priya at 500.

Step 4: The barrier reaches the merge operator on the retail input first. The merge operator records that retail is barriered, one of two inputs aligned, and stops treating further retail records as pre-checkpoint. A post-barrier retail transaction of 50 then arrives, and because retail has already barriered, the merge operator buffers it rather than counting it in this checkpoint.

Step 5: A corporate transaction of 700 arrives before the corporate barrier, so it is pre-barrier and is counted into the merged state. Then the barrier arrives on the corporate input, making two of two inputs aligned. Now the merge operator snapshots a consistent state that includes all pre-barrier records from both inputs and excludes the buffered post-barrier record, acknowledges to the coordinator, and drains the buffered record.

Step 6: With both operators acknowledged, the coordinator declares checkpoint one complete and records its metadata, making it a valid recovery point. A crash is then simulated by clearing the balance operator's state, and restore rebuilds it from the snapshot, bringing Rajesh back to 1000, proving the job can resume from the consistent cut.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Coordinator TRIGGER checkpoint 1
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] BalanceOperator snapshot ckpt=1 state={SAV2001=1000, CUR3001=500}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] MergeOperator received barrier on retail (1/2 aligned)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] MergeOperator received barrier on corporate (2/2 aligned)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] MergeOperator ALIGNED ckpt=1 snapshot mergedCount=2
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Coordinator checkpoint 1 COMPLETE (all acked)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Checkpoint complete? true
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] --- simulating crash + restore ---
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] BalanceOperator restored state={SAV2001=1000, CUR3001=500}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Recovered SAV2001 = 1000
```

  ═══ LLD — Barrier Snapshot Protocol ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshot (barrier marker)          │
  │   WHY: consistent global cut without stopping the stream      │
  │ Observer Pattern: operators ack the coordinator               │
  │   WHY: coordinator declares complete when all report          │

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: coordinator coordinates; operators snapshot their own state│
  │ O: new operator type = new snapshot impl, protocol unchanged  │
  │ L: any operator plugs into trigger/ack/restore                │
  │ I: acknowledge/restore are narrow contracts                   │
  │ D: coordinator depends on ack messages, not operator internals│

  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ BalanceOperator  │  │ MergeOperator (2 inputs)  │
  │ (1 input)        │  │ - barrieredInputs: Set    │

  │ + process()      │  │ + process(input,r,coord)  │
  │ + restore()      │  │   ALIGNMENT logic         │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Barrier Alignment (2-input op) ─────────────

  [WAITING] ──barrier on input A──→ [ALIGNING: buffer A's records]
       │                                   │
       │ barrier on input B                │ barrier on input B
       ▼                                   ▼
  [ALIGNED] → snapshot → ack → drain buffer → [WAITING next ckpt]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────────

  1. coordinator.triggerCheckpoint() → id=1, inject barrier
  2. balanceOp.process(barrier) → snapshot {SAV=1000,CUR=500}, ack
  3. mergeOp.process("retail", barrier) → 1/2 aligned
  4. mergeOp.process("retail", txn50) → BUFFERED (post-barrier)

  6. coordinator all acked → COMPLETE

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink checkpointing is a distributed snapshot mechanism based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm, and the key to understanding it is the barrier. The checkpoint coordinator in the JobManager periodically triggers a checkpoint by telling every source to inject a special marker called a barrier, carrying a checkpoint id, into its output stream. The barrier is not data; it is a separator that divides the records belonging before the checkpoint from those belonging after it, and it flows downstream through the dataflow graph alongside normal records, never overtaking them. As each operator receives the barrier, it snapshots its own state and forwards the barrier onward. When every operator has acknowledged its snapshot to the coordinator, the checkpoint is complete and represents one globally consistent cut of the entire distributed job.

The subtle part is barrier alignment for operators with multiple inputs, such as after a join or a union. When the barrier arrives on one input, the operator stops consuming that input and buffers its further records, while it keeps consuming the other inputs until their barriers for the same checkpoint arrive too. Only when barriers have arrived on all inputs does the operator snapshot, which guarantees the snapshot contains exactly all pre-barrier records and none of the post-barrier ones, giving a consistent state. The snapshot itself is uploaded asynchronously to durable storage like S3 or HDFS, so the processing thread is barely blocked. On failure, Flink restores every operator from the last completed checkpoint and rewinds the sources to the offsets stored in it, resuming from a consistent point with exactly-once state semantics. Two senior points matter: alignment can amplify backpressure because fast inputs wait on slow ones, which is why unaligned checkpoints exist, and exactly-once end to end additionally needs transactional or idempotent sinks, because checkpointing guarantees consistent state, not consistent external side effects.

At the National Bank of India this was the backbone of our stateful running-balance job. We enabled checkpointing every ten seconds in exactly-once mode with S3 checkpoint storage, so that if a task manager crashed, every account balance and every source offset were restored to one coherent instant, never losing or double-applying a transaction, which is non-negotiable for money. We had an operator that merged the retail and corporate transaction streams, and barrier alignment there was exactly what ensured its snapshot captured all pre-barrier records from both streams and excluded post-barrier ones, so the merged state was consistent. We paired this with a transactional sink so the whole pipeline was exactly-once end to end, and we watched checkpoint duration and alignment buffering time as metrics, because long alignment meant backpressure we needed to address. Being able to explain barriers, alignment, asynchronous snapshots, coordinator acknowledgments, and the role of transactional sinks is precisely what demonstrates that you truly understand how Flink achieves fault tolerance.
